Part 1 of 4

Nose cone

Shaped to cut through the air with as little drag as possible. At apogee the ejection charge pushes it off the front, and the eyebolt at the center of its base ties it to the shock cord so it stays with the rocket.

Part 2 of 4

Recovery bay

The parachute is folded tight and wrapped in its shock cord and shroud lines, and rides inside the top of the airframe. When the nose cone is pushed off at apogee the chute pulls out, and the cord keeps the nose cone, parachute and airframe tied together.

Part 3 of 4

Airframe

One white fiberglass tube carries the loads from nose to tail, with the parachute packed into its top. Rail buttons guide it up the launch rail, and epoxy fillets bond the three plywood fins to its base. The motor slides in from the back.

Part 4 of 4

Motor

A single-use solid-propellant motor sits inside the airframe tube, held in by a retainer ring at the tail. Its size and burn time set how high the rocket flies.
